faq.q: What is the most common type of TEF?

exam: What bedside signs would make you suspect a tracheoesophageal fistula in a newborn? — Look for drooling, choking on feeds, cyanosis that improves when the infant is placed on the side of the lesion, and inability to pass an NGT beyond 10 cm.

How does the Gross classification influence surgical planning? — Type C (most common) requires ligation of the distal fistula and primary oesophageal anastomosis; other types may need different approaches or staged repairs.

If a chest X‑ray shows a coiled NGT but no air in the stomach, what is the next investigation and why? — Perform a contrast oesophagography to confirm the presence or absence of a distal fistula, because air may be absent despite a small fistula.

What immediate measures should be taken before the infant reaches the operating theatre? — Position prone or on the side of the fistula, keep the airway clear with suction, start IV fluids, and give broad‑spectrum antibiotics to cover aspiration pneumonia.

Why is a gastrostomy sometimes placed before definitive repair in low‑resource settings? — It provides nutrition when the oesophagus cannot be used and avoids prolonged malnutrition while waiting for surgical resources.

What postoperative complication should you monitor for on day 3 and how would you detect it? — Anastomotic leak; look for increasing chest drainage, fever, tachypnoea, and confirm with contrast swallow if the infant tolerates feeds.

How would you differentiate a tracheoesophageal fistula from a laryngeal cleft on examination? — In a laryngeal cleft the NGT passes into the stomach and the cough is triggered by secretions, whereas in TEF the NGT coils and coughing occurs with each swallow.

Why are proton‑pump inhibitors used after repair, and what are the risks in neonates? — They reduce acid reflux that can damage the anastomosis; however, long‑term use may increase infection risk and affect calcium absorption, so limit duration.
ai.title: Tracheoesophageal Fistula
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: A tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) is an abnormal connection between the trachea and oesophagus, most often seen with oesophageal atresia in newborns. In low‑resource settings, diagnosis relies on clinical clues and basic imaging, and timely surgical repair is essential to prevent aspiration and death.

b: Coiled NGT on X‑ray suggests OA/TEF
Air in stomach indicates a distal fistula
sections.p: A congenital TEF is a direct communication between the tracheal lumen and the oesophagus, usually accompanying oesophageal atresia (OA). Diagnosis is clinical, supported by a nasogastric tube (NGT) that coils in the upper pouch and by plain chest X‑ray showing air in the stomach.

b: Type A: isolated OA
Type B: proximal fistula, distal OA
Type C: proximal OA, distal fistula (most common)
Type D: both proximal and distal fistulae
Type E: isolated fistula (no atresia)
sections.p: The most widely used classification is the Gross (or Vogt) system, describing five anatomical types; type C (proximal OA with distal fistula) accounts for >85 % of cases and guides surgical planning.

b: Failure of trachea‑oesophageal septation (primary cause)
Maternal rubella or other viral infections
VACTERL association (vertebral, cardiac, renal anomalies)
Chromosomal anomalies (trisomy 18, 21)
Environmental teratogens (e.g., certain herbal medicines)
sections.p: TEF is a developmental error during foregut separation (weeks 4‑6). In low‑resource regions, associated factors include maternal infections (e.g., rubella), exposure to teratogens, and genetic syndromes such as VACTERL association.

b: Drooling and inability to swallow saliva
Cough or gagging with each feed
Cyanosis that resolves when lying on the side of the fistula
Failure to pass NGT into the stomach
sections.p: Newborns with TEF present with excessive drooling, choking, coughing during feeds, and cyanosis that improves when the infant is placed prone. A nasogastric tube cannot be passed beyond 10‑15 cm.

t.b: Shows position of NGT tip and presence of air in stomach
Confirms location of atresia and fistula
Detects associated renal anomalies in VACTERL
Screens for cardiac defects common in VACTERL

b: Persistent respiratory distress after feeds
Fever, tachypnoea, crackles indicating aspiration pneumonia
Weight loss >10 % of birth weight in first week
Severe hypoxia requiring ventilation
sections.p: Uncorrected TEF leads to recurrent aspiration pneumonia, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and severe malnutrition. Early sepsis is a life‑threatening emergency.

b: Place infant prone or on side of fistula; keep head low
Continuous suction of oropharynx and nasogastric tube
Start parenteral fluids; consider nasogastric feeding distal to atresia if possible
Surgical repair: right posterolateral thoracotomy (or extrapleural) with fistula ligation and oesophageal anastomosis (type C)
Post‑op: gentle ventilation, monitor for leaks, start feeds after contrast study
sections.p: Stabilise airway, prevent aspiration, then surgically close the fistula. Pre‑operative care focuses on positioning, suction, and nutrition via gastrostomy if needed.

t.a: Proton‑pump inhibitor (e.g., omeprazole) if reflux suspected
t.b: Reduces gastric acidity to protect anastomosis

b: Weekly weight checks until stable gain
Contrast swallow study before oral feeds (usually day 5‑7 post‑op)
Endoscopic dilatation for anastomotic stricture
Vaccinate against pneumococcus and influenza to reduce respiratory infections
sections.p: Long‑term follow‑up monitors growth, swallowing function, and respiratory health. Early detection of stricture or recurrent fistula is essential.

b: Laryngeal cleft: similar cough but NGT passes into stomach
Tracheal stenosis: stridor without feeding difficulty
Severe reflux: vomiting without NGT coiling
sections.p: Conditions that mimic TEF include laryngeal cleft, tracheal stenosis, and severe gastro‑oesophageal reflux causing choking.

b: Air in stomach without fistula – consider vigorous suction or bag‑mask ventilation before imaging
Normal chest X‑ray does not exclude a tiny fistula; persistent symptoms warrant contrast study
sections.p: A small amount of air in the stomach on X‑ray may be misinterpreted as a distal fistula when it can arise from swallowed air; clinical correlation is mandatory.

whenToSeekHelp: Cyanosis that does not improve with positioning
Rapid respiratory deterioration or apnea after feeds
Fever with tachypnoea indicating aspiration pneumonia
